facts.largest_city: Los Angeles (the second-largest city in the U.S.)
facts.statehood_note: California joined the Union as a free state under the Compromise of 1850; its first constitution (1849) banned slavery.
facts.motto: Eureka (Greek for "I have found it!"), on the state seal since 1849 and the official motto since 1963

symbols.name: California redwood: coast redwood and giant sequoia (1953)
California grizzly bear (1953), which went extinct by the 1920s

facts.name_origin: Most likely from the make-believe island of California, ruled by Queen Calafia, in the Spanish adventure book Las Sergas de Esplandián (1510) by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo.

government.chambers: California State Senate (40 members, 4-year terms, with half elected every two years) and California State Assembly (80 members, 2-year terms). A legislator may serve 12 years in total across both houses.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; may be elected no more than twice). The governor is one of 12 statewide elected officers, each limited to two four-year terms. The Lieutenant Governor presides over the Senate, breaks tie votes, and acts as governor when the governor cannot serve or is out of the state.
government.courts: Supreme Court of California (7 justices: a chief justice and six associate justices) is the highest court. Below it are the Courts of Appeal in six appellate districts and one superior court in each of the 58 counties.
government.local: 58 counties. California's 109 federally recognized tribes are sovereign nations with their own governments.
government.constitution: California's first constitution was written at a convention in Monterey in September 1849, in both English and Spanish, by delegates who included Californios such as Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo; it banned slavery, and voters ratified it on November 13, 1849. The current constitution was ratified on May 7, 1879, took effect January 1, 1880, and has been amended so many times that it is one of the longest constitutions in the world.
government.kid_line: "Rights guaranteed by this Constitution are not dependent on those guaranteed by the United States Constitution." (California Constitution, Article I, Section 24)

long_ago.about: Before Spanish settlement, at least 300,000 Indigenous people lived in California in more than 70 ethnic groups. Together they spoke more than 100 languages.
The Yurok live where the lower Klamath River meets the Pacific Ocean. Salmon are at the heart of Yurok life; one scholar calls salmon "the essence of Yurok existence."
The Karuk live along the middle Klamath River and are known as the salmon and acorn people, because their way of life has long depended on those foods.

The Tongva lived in villages such as Jachivit, near what became Mission San Gabriel. Women were central to their spiritual life, medicine people were paid with gifts such as beads, and each fall a Mourning Ceremony with dances honored the dead.

first_peoples.today_note: A state list dated February 27, 2026, counts 109 federally recognized tribes in California. Some nations, such as the Kizh, in which Toypurina's descendants are enrolled, are not on that list. In 2019 the state formally apologized for the genocide, displacement, and mistreatment of California Native peoples (Executive Order N-15-19) and created a Native American-led Truth and Healing Council.

Mission San Gabriel (where Toypurina helped plan the 1785 revolt against Spanish mission rule)
Petaluma Adobe (Mariano Vallejo's ranch, built 1836 to 1844, where up to 2,000 workers, many of them Native Americans, labored)

history.event: At least 300,000 Indigenous people in more than 70 groups live in California, speaking more than 100 languages.
On September 28, the Spanish expedition of Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo sails into San Diego Bay.
Gaspar de Portolá and Father Junípero Serra found Mission San Diego de Alcalá and the Presidio of San Diego; Spain colonizes California from 1769 to 1821.
After Spain bans Native dances at the missions (1782), the Tongva medicine woman Toypurina and Nicolás José plan a revolt at Mission San Gabriel; it is betrayed, and she is captured.
Mexico wins independence from Spain, and California comes under Mexican rule.
By this year Mexico has secularized the missions (ended church control). At Sonoma, Mariano Vallejo first gives some mission land to Native mission workers but later takes all of it for himself.

In the Bear Flag Revolt, American settlers arrest Vallejo on June 10 and jail him at Sutter's Fort as the U.S. invades California. By now the Native population has fallen from about 300,000 to about 100,000.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (February 2) gives California to the United States, and gold is found at Sutter's Mill, starting the Gold Rush; prospectors arrive from around the world.
Delegates, including Californios, write a constitution in English and Spanish at Monterey that bans slavery; voters ratify it on November 13.
California becomes the 31st state on September 9, entering as a free state under the Compromise of 1850.

Massacres, land seizures, and state bounties kill thousands of Native Californians (one historian estimates 9,492 to 16,092 people, including some killed by the U.S. Army); in 1851 the governor openly predicts "a war of extermination." By 1900 fewer than 20,000 Native Californians survive, and today the state calls this a genocide.
In January, a Los Angeles court frees Biddy Mason and her family, whom enslaver Robert Smith had planned to take to Texas, because California's constitution bans slavery.
During the Civil War, California stays in the Union and ships gold east to support it, even though a large pro-Southern group lives in the state.

trailblazers.name: Toypurina
trailblazers.group: Tongva woman, medicine woman and resistance leader
trailblazers.text: Toypurina, a Tongva medicine woman from the village of Jachivit, recruited leaders from six villages for a 1785 revolt at Mission San Gabriel after the Spanish banned Native dances. The plan was betrayed, she was captured and convicted, and she was banished to a distant mission. A soldier recorded that she "was angry with the Padres and the others of the Mission."

trailblazers.name: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo
trailblazers.group: Californio (Mexican Californian) man, military leader and lawmaker
trailblazers.text: Born in Monterey, Vallejo rose to command Mexican forces in Alta California and ran a huge ranch at Petaluma where up to 2,000 workers, many of them Native Americans, labored; he led soldiers against the Miwok in 1829 and took Sonoma mission lands for himself. At the 1849 constitutional convention he supported making slavery illegal, Indian voting rights, and property rights for wives, and he became one of California's first state senators. He later lost most of his land to U.S. courts and squatters.

trailblazers.name: Biddy Mason
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, nurse, landowner, and church founder
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery, Biddy Mason walked about 1,700 miles west with her enslaver's wagon train. In January 1856 a Los Angeles judge freed her and her family under California's ban on slavery. Working as a nurse and midwife, she bought land in what is now downtown Los Angeles in 1866 and in 1872 helped found the city's First African Methodist Episcopal Church, which first met in her home.

trailblazers.name: Mary Tape
trailblazers.group: Chinese American woman, civil rights fighter and artist
trailblazers.text: Brought from China to San Francisco as an orphan at age 11, Mary Tape and her husband Joseph sued when a public school turned away their daughter Mamie for being Chinese. They won Tape v. Hurley in 1885, and Mary wrote a famous letter to the school board asking, "Is it a disgrace to be born a Chinese?" She was also a painter, photographer, and telegrapher.

trailblazers.name: Mamie Tape
trailblazers.text: In 1884, when she was 8, Mamie Tape was refused entry to Spring Valley Primary School in San Francisco because she was Chinese. In March 1885 the California Supreme Court ruled that public schools must be open to "all children," but the state then allowed separate Chinese schools, and Mamie and her brother Frank became the first students at the Chinese Primary School. That separate-school law was finally repealed in 1947.

trailblazers.name: Fred Korematsu
trailblazers.group: Japanese American man, civil rights hero
trailblazers.text: Born in Oakland, Fred Korematsu refused at age 23 to report to the camps when the U.S. government ordered Japanese Americans removed from their homes in 1942. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 against him in 1944, but a federal court in San Francisco overturned his conviction on November 10, 1983. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1998, and since 2010 California has marked Fred Korematsu Day every January 30.

trailblazers.name: Sylvia Mendez
trailblazers.group: Mexican and Puerto Rican American woman, civil rights activist
trailblazers.text: Sylvia Mendez's parents, Gonzalo Mendez (from Mexico) and Felicitas Mendez (from Puerto Rico), joined four other families in a 1945 lawsuit after Orange County schools in Westminster separated Mexican American children; Sylvia was eight. A federal judge ruled for the families in 1946, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed in 1947, and Governor Earl Warren then signed a law ending school segregation in California. Many of the case's arguments were later used in Brown v. Board of Education, and Sylvia received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011.

landforms: Sierra Nevada (with Mount Whitney, 14,505 feet, the highest peak in the lower 48 states)
Coast Ranges, Cascade Range, and Tehachapi Mountains
Death Valley (Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America, about 280 feet below sea level)
White Mountains (home of ancient bristlecone pines)
waters: Sacramento River and San Joaquin River (meet in the Delta)
Clear Lake (largest freshwater lake entirely in California)
Salton Sea (a large inland salt lake)
geography.regions: California has a long Pacific coast and Coast Ranges in the west, the flat Central Valley in the middle, the Sierra Nevada and Cascade mountains in the east and north, and the Mojave Desert and Death Valley in the southeast.

ecosystems.name: Redwood and sequoia forests
ecosystems.about: About 45% of California is forest. Coast redwoods are the tallest trees and giant sequoias are the largest; the Grizzly Giant sequoia in Yosemite is 209 feet tall.

ecosystems.name: Klamath River and salmon
ecosystems.about: Salmon swim up the Klamath River, and the Yurok and Karuk peoples have depended on them for generations. Removing four dams is expected to reopen about 400 miles of salmon habitat.

ecosystems.name: Oak woodlands
ecosystems.about: The California valley quail, the state bird, lives in oak woodlands and brush, gathering in flocks of 30 to 300 birds outside nesting season, with one male keeping watch as a sentry.

ecosystems.name: Deserts
ecosystems.about: Death Valley recorded 134°F on July 10, 1913, the hottest temperature on record in the world, and the desert tortoise is the state reptile. Nearby, some bristlecone pines in the White Mountains are over 5,000 years old.

science.weather: Most of California has a Mediterranean climate, with alpine weather in the mountains. The state has about two-thirds of the nation's earthquake risk (about 37,000 earthquakes are recorded each year), along with droughts, wildfires, and Santa Ana winds; the 2011 to 2017 drought was the worst on record.
science.resources: California has the largest economy of any state and leads the nation in farm products, especially dairy, almonds, and grapes. It also produces oil (mostly in Kern County), runs the busiest U.S. port at Los Angeles, and is home to Hollywood and Silicon Valley; gold, found in 1848, is the state mineral.
science.highlight: The San Andreas Fault, more than 800 miles long, is where the Pacific Plate slides northwest past the North American Plate by as much as 2 inches a year; in the April 18, 1906, San Francisco earthquake, a road at Tomales Bay was shifted almost 21 feet.

g3_ss.title: California's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Sacramento, Los Angeles, the 58 counties, and tribal nations; learn what the governor, the 120-member Legislature, and the 7-justice Supreme Court do; discuss the motto "Eureka" and Article I, Section 24.

g3_ss.title: California's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Learn that more than 100 languages were spoken in California, meet the salmon peoples of the Klamath River (Yurok and Karuk) and the Tongva, whose villages joined Toypurina's revolt, and find out that 109 tribes are federally recognized today.

g3_ss.title: California Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Toypurina, Mariano Vallejo, Biddy Mason, and Mary and Mamie Tape, and talk about how each stood up for themselves or their community.

g45_ss.title: California's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study how California's many nations lived before 1769, then look honestly at how missions, the Gold Rush, and state violence cut the Native population, and at the 2019 state apology.

g45_ss.title: Spanish and Mexican California
g45_ss.plan: Follow Cabrillo (1542), the missions from 1769, Toypurina's 1785 revolt, Mexican rule from 1821, mission secularization, and the Californio ranchos of leaders like Vallejo.

g45_ss.title: California 1846 to 1877
g45_ss.plan: Trace the Bear Flag Revolt, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the Gold Rush, the 1849 bilingual constitution, free-state admission in 1850, Biddy Mason's freedom case, and California's Civil War role.

g3_sci.title: Giant Trees
g3_sci.plan: Compare coast redwoods, giant sequoias, and bristlecone pines by height, size, and age, using string to measure out a 209-foot tree on the playground.

g3_sci.title: Salmon Journeys
g3_sci.plan: Follow a salmon's life cycle up the Klamath River and learn why removing dams helps salmon return.

g3_sci.title: California's State Animals
g3_sci.plan: Study the valley quail, the desert tortoise, and the extinct California grizzly bear, and talk about why animals can disappear.

g45_sci.title: Earthquakes and the San Andreas Fault
g45_sci.plan: Model two plates sliding past each other with blocks, measure 2 inches a year over many years, and practice earthquake safety.

g45_sci.title: Extreme Heat and Drought
g45_sci.plan: Graph Death Valley temperatures, investigate drought and wildfire, and design ways to save water.

g45_sci.title: Landforms from Whitney to Badwater
g45_sci.plan: Build a relief map from Mount Whitney (14,505 feet) to Badwater Basin (below sea level) and explain how mountains and valleys shape weather and farming.
